mainEntity.name: Is a 30% markup the same as a 30% margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Markup is a share of your cost, margin is a share of your price. A 30% markup leaves a 23.1% margin, because the profit is divided by the larger number.
$120. The $20 of profit is 20% of the $100 cost but only 16.7% of the $120 price, which is the margin you would report.

mainEntity.name: How do you convert a margin into a markup?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flip the toggle from markup to margin and type the target. Ask for 33% here and it prints a $31.24 price, a 54% markup on your $20.30 landed cost. The textbook conversion says 49.3%, and the gap is the 3% shrink sitting between cost and price.

mainEntity.name: What should a markup be applied to?

acceptedAnswer.text: Landed cost, not the supplier invoice. An $18.00 case with $1.40 freight and $0.90 handling costs you $20.30, and marking up the $18.00 leaves $2.30 a case unrecovered.

mainEntity.name: How does shrink change the margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: It raises the cost of everything you do sell. At 3%, a $20.30 landed cost behaves like $20.93, which turns a 31.0% paper margin into 28.9%.

mainEntity.name: Why does a 45% markup leave under 29%?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two reasons compound. Markup measured on price is always smaller, which takes 45% to 31.0%, and then 3% shrink takes it to 28.9%.

mainEntity.name: Should targets be set in markup or margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Margin. It is the number that appears in your accounts, and it cannot be misread. Convert to a markup once, write it down, and have every rep use the same one.
